text: It is hard to get direct evidence of prospective reasoning in animals. <break time="0.8s" /> But there is now good behavioral evidence of capacities that, in humans, would be enabled by prospection. <break time="0.8s" /> Most of this work has been done with corvids and with great apes. <break time="0.8s" /> For instance, animals from both groups can solve the floating peanut problem, seemingly by insight rather than trial and error. <break time="0.8s" /> This is the problem of how to reach a food item that is too far down in a clear, fixed tube to be reached by hand or beak. <break time="0.8s" /> The solution is to spit water into the tube in the case of the chimps, or to drop stones into the tube that already contains some water in the case of the rooks, so as to float the item far enough up to be reached. <break time="0.8s" /> The same problem is solved by most 8 year old human children, but by hardly any 4 year olds. <break time="0.8s" /> Rationally, it seems that one solves this problem by imagining various things one might do with the available materials until one hits on the correct solution. <break time="0.8s" /> We do not know that the animals in question achieve their insights in the same way, of course, but the simplest hypothesis is that they do.
